nodes.name: Limit-preserving functors lift to over categories
nodes.statement: Let $J$ be a shape (i.e. a category). Let $\widetilde J$ denote the category which is the same as $J$, but has an extra object $*$ which is terminal. If $F : C \to D$ is a functor preserving limits of shape $\widetilde J$, then the obvious functor $C / X \to D / F(X)$ preserves limits of shape $J$.

nodes.name: Fully faithful product-preserving functors lift to monoid/group objects
nodes.statement: If a finite-products-preserving functor $F : C \to D$ is fully faithful, then so is $\mathrm{Grp}(F) : \mathrm{Grp} C \to \mathrm{Grp} D$.

nodes.name: A fully faithful functor product-preserving is a group isomorphism on hom sets
nodes.statement: If $F : C \to D$ is a fully faithful functor between cartesian-monoidal categories and $X, G \in C$ are an object and a group object respectively, then $\mathrm{Grp}(F) : (X \hom G) \hom \backcong (F(X) \hom F(G))$ is a group isomorphism.

nodes.name: Pulling back a module object
nodes.statement: Let $M, N$ be two monoid objects in a monoidal category $C$. Let $f : M \to N$ be a monoid morphism. If $X$ is a $N$-module object, then it is also a $M$-module object.
nodes.label: 0-comap-mod

nodes.name: The tensor product of linearly independent families
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a domain and $M, N$ two $R$-semimodules. If $f$ and $g$ are linearly independent families of points in $M$ and $N$, then $(i, j) \mapsto f i \otimes g j$ is a linearly independent family of points in $M \otimes N$.
nodes.label: 0-tensor-lin-indep

nodes.statement: We will prove the equivalent statement: Let $P, Q$ be two free $R$ modules, $f : P \to M$ and $g : Q \to N$ be two $R$-linear injective maps. Then $f \otimes g : P \otimes_R Q \to M \otimes_R N$ is injective. Let $K$ be the field of fractions of $R$. The map \[ P \otimes_R Q \to (K \otimes_R P) \otimes_R (K \otimes_R Q) = (K \otimes_R P) \otimes_K (K \otimes_R Q) \] is injective because $R \to K$ is injective and all the modules involved are flat. The map \[ (K \otimes_R P) \otimes_K (K \otimes_R Q) \to (K \otimes_R M) \otimes_K (K \otimes_R N) \] is injective because all the modules involved are $K$-flat (as $K$ is a field). $P \otimes_R Q \to M \otimes_R N$ is now a factor of the composition of the two injections above, and is thus is injective.

nodes.name: Affine monoid
nodes.statement: An \emph{affine monoid} is a finitely generated commutative monoid which is: \begin{itemize} \item cancellative: if $a + c = b + c$ then $a = b$, and \item torsion-free: if $n a = n b$ then $a = b$ (for $n \geq 1$). \end{itemize}
nodes.label: 0-aff-mon

nodes.name: Embedding an affine monoid inside a lattice
nodes.statement: If $M$ is an affine monoid, then $M$ can be embedded inside ${\mathbb Z}^n$ for some $n$.
nodes.label: 0-embed-aff-mon

nodes.statement: Embed $M$ inside its Grothendieck group $G$. Prove that $G$ is finitely generated free.

nodes.name: Affine monoid algebras are domains
nodes.statement: If $R$ is an integral domain $M$ is an affine monoid, then $R[M]$ is an integral domain and is a finitely generated $R$-algebra.
nodes.label: 0-aff-mon-alg-domain

nodes.statement: $i : R[M] \hookrightarrow R[{\mathbb Z} M]$ injects into an integral domain so is an integral domain. It's finitely generated by $\chi^{a_i}$ where $\mathcal A = \{a_1, \dotsc, a_s\}$ is a finite generating set for $M$.

nodes.name: Irreducible element
nodes.statement: An element $x$ of a monoid $M$ is \emph{irreducible} if $x = y + z$ implies $y = 0$ or $z = 0$.
nodes.label: 0-irred

nodes.name: Irreducible elements lie in all sets generating a salient monoid
nodes.statement: If $M$ is a monoid with a single unit, and $S$ is a set generating $M$, then $S$ contains all irreducible elements of $M$.
nodes.label: 0-irred-subset-gen

nodes.statement: Assume $p$ is an irreducible element. Since $S$ generates $M$, write \[ p = \sum_i a_i \] where the $a_i$ are finitely many elements (not necessarily distinct) elements of $S$. Since $p$ is irreducible, we must have \[ p = a_i \in S \] for some $i$.

nodes.name: A salient finitely generated monoid has finitely many irreducible elements
nodes.statement: If $M$ is a finitely generated monoid with a single unit, then only finitely many elements of $M$ are irreducible.
nodes.label: 0-irred-finite

nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a finite set generating $M$. Write $I$ the set of irreducible elements. By Proposition \ref{0-irred-subset-gen}, $I \subseteq S$. Hence $I$ is finite.

nodes.name: A salient finitely generated cancellative monoid is generated by its irreducible elements
nodes.statement: If $M$ is a finitely generated cancellative monoid with a single unit, then $M$ is generated by its irreducible elements.
nodes.label: 0-irred-gen

nodes.statement: We do not follow the proof from \cite{Cox_2011}. Let $S$ be a finite minimal generating set and assume for contradiction that $r \in S$ is reducible, say $r = a + b$ where $a, b$ are non-units. Write \[a = \sum_{s \in S} m_s s, b = \sum_{s \in S} n_s s\] for some $m_s, n_s \in {\mathbb N}$, so that \[r = \sum_{s \in S} (m_s + n_s) s.\] We distinguish three cases \begin{itemize} \item $m_r + n_r = 0$. Then \[r = \sum_{s \in S \setminus \{r\}} (m_s + n_s) s \in \langle S \setminus \{r\}\rangle\] contradicting the minimality of $S$. \item $m_r + n_r = 1$. Then \begin{align*} & 0 = \sum_{s \in S \setminus \{r\}} (m_s + n_s) s & \implies \forall s \in S \setminus \{r\}, m_s s = n_s s = 0 \end{align*} Furthermore, either $m_r = 0$ or $n_r = 0$, so $a = 0$ or $b = 0$, contradicting the fact that $a$ and $b$ are non-units. \item $m_r + n_r \ge 2$. Then \[0 = r + \sum_{s \in S \setminus \{r\}} (m_s + n_s) s\] and $r = 0$, contradicting the minimality of $S$ once again. \end{itemize}

nodes.name: Coideal
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $(C,\Delta,\varepsilon)$ be a coalgebra over $R$. An $R$-submodule $I$ of $C$ is a \emph{coideal} of $C$ if $\Delta(I) \subseteq \bar{I \otimes_R C} + \bar{C \otimes_R I}$ and $\varepsilon(I)=0$, where $\bar{\cdot}$ denotes the image in $C \otimes_R C$.
nodes.label: 0-coideal

nodes.name: Quotient coalgebra
nodes.statement: If $C$ is a coalgebra over $R$ and $I$ is a coideal, the quotient $C /I$ is equipped with a canonical $R$-coalgebra structure.
nodes.label: 0-coquot

nodes.statement: Straightforward.

nodes.name: Quotient coalgebra map
nodes.statement: If $C$ is a coalgebra over $R$ and $I$ is a coideal, the quotient map $C \to C / I$ is a coalgebra homomorphism.
nodes.label: 0-coquot-hom

nodes.statement: Straightforward.

nodes.name: Bialgebra ideal
nodes.statement: Let $B$ be a bialgebra over a commutative ring $R$. A \emph{bialgebra ideal} $I$ is an ideal which is also a coideal.
nodes.label: 0-biideal

nodes.name: Quotient bialgebra
nodes.statement: If $B$ is a bialgebra over $R$ and $I$ is a bialgebra ideal, the quotient $B / I$ is equipped with a canonical $R$-bialgebra structure.
nodes.label: 0-biquot

nodes.statement: Straightforward.

nodes.name: Quotient bialgebra map
nodes.statement: If $B$ is a bialgebra over $R$ and $I$ is a bialgebra ideal, the quotient map $B \to B / I$ is a bialgebra homomorphism.
nodes.label: 0-biquot-hom

nodes.statement: Straightforward.

nodes.name: Hopf ideal
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a Hopf algebra over a commutative ring $R$. A \emph{Hopf ideal} $I$ is a bialgebra ideal such that $S(I)=I$.
nodes.label: 0-hopf-ideal

nodes.name: Quotient Hopf algebra
nodes.statement: If $A$ is a Hopf algebra over $R$ and $I$ is a Hopf ideal, the quotient $A / I$ is equipped with a canonical Hopf algebra structure over $R$.
nodes.label: 0-hopf-quot

nodes.statement: Straightforward.

nodes.name: Quotient Hopf algebra map
nodes.statement: If $A$ is a Hopf algebra over $R$ and $I$ is a Hopf ideal, the quotient map $A \to A / I$ is a Hopf algebra homomorphism.
nodes.label: 0-hopf-quot-hom

nodes.statement: Follows immediately from Proposition \ref{0-biquot-hom}.

nodes.name: Freeness of group algebras under an injective hom
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring. Let $G, H$ be abelian groups and $f : G \to H$ an injective group hom. Then $R[H]$ is a free $R[G]$-module.
nodes.label: 0-grp-alg-free

nodes.statement: Pick a section $\sigma : H / f(G) \to H$ and the unique map $\varphi : H \to G$ such that $h = \sigma(h f(G)) f(\varphi(h))$. We claim that $R[H]$ is isomorphic to $R[G]^{\oplus H / f(G)}$, from which the result follows, as such: \begin{align*} R[G]^{\oplus H / f(G)} & \simeq R[H] \\ \varphi(h) e_{h f(G)} & \mapsto h g e_x & \mapsfrom \sigma(x) f(g) \end{align*} Those two functions are clearly inverse to each other, and the forward map is clearly $R[G]$-linear.

nodes.name: The kernel of a map on direct sums
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be an abelian group generated by a set $S$. Let $A, B$ be arbitrary indexing types and $f : A \to B$ a function. Write $f^\oplus : G^{\oplus A} \to G^{\oplus B}$ the pushforward. Then \[ \ker f^\oplus = \mathrm{span}\{gX^a_1 - gX^a_2 | g \in S, a_1, a_2 \in A, f(a_1) = f(a_2)\}. \]
nodes.label: 0-ker-mon-alg

nodes.statement: Write $I = \mathrm{span}\{gX^a_1 - gX^a_2 | g \in G, a_1, a_2 \in A, f(a_1) = f(a_2)\}$ for brevity. Note that we can assume WLOG that $f$ is surjective. Write $\sigma : B \to A$ a section of $f$. Let's prove by induction on $x \in G^\oplus A$ that $\sigma^\oplus(f^\oplus(x)) \equiv x \mod I$: \begin{itemize} \item $x = 0$: $\sigma^\oplus(f^\oplus(0)) = 0$ \item $x = gX^a$: $\sigma^\oplus(f^\oplus(gX^a)) = gX^{\sigma(f(a))} \equiv gX^a \mod I$ as $S$ generates \item $x + y$: Assume the induction hypothesis for $x$ and $y$. Then \[ \sigma^\oplus(f^\oplus(x + y)) = \sigma^\oplus(f^\oplus(x)) + \sigma^\oplus(f^\oplus(y)) \equiv x + y \mod I \] \end{itemize} Now, for any $x \in G^\oplus A$, \[ x \in \ker f^\oplus \iff f^\oplus(x) = 0 \iff \sigma^\oplus(f^\oplus(x)) \equiv 0 \mod I \iff x \equiv 0 \mod I \] and we are done.

nodes.name: Localising a monoid algebra
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring. Let $M$ be a commutative monoid and $M'$ be its localization at some $S \subseteq M$. Then $R[M']$ is the localization of $R[M]$ at $\mathrm{span} \{X^s | s \in S\}$.
nodes.label: 0-loc-mon-alg

nodes.statement: Straightforward.

nodes.name: Group-like elements
nodes.statement: An element $a$ of a coalgebra $A$ is \emph{group-like} if $\eta(a) = 1$ and $\Delta(a) = a \otimes a$, where $\eta$ is the counit and $\Delta$ is the comultiplication map. We write $\mathrm{GrpLike} A$ for the set of group-like elements of $A$.
nodes.label: 0-grp-like

nodes.name: Group-like elements form a group
nodes.statement: Group-like elements $\mathrm{GrpLike} A$ of a bialgebra $A$ form a monoid. Group-like elements $\mathrm{GrpLike} A$ of a Hopf algebra $A$ form a group.
nodes.label: 0-grp-like-grp

nodes.statement: Check that group-like elements are closed under unit, multiplication and inverses.

nodes.name: Bialgebra homs preserve group-like elements
nodes.statement: Let $f : A \to B$ be a bi-algebra hom. If $a \in A$ is group-like, then $f(a)$ is group-like too.
nodes.label: 0-grp-like-map

nodes.statement: $a$ is a unit, so $f(a)$ is a unit too. Then \[ f(a) \otimes f(a) = (f \otimes f)(\Delta_A(a)) = \Delta_B(f(a)) \] so $f(a)$ is group-like.
If $R$ is a commutative semiring, $A$ is a Hopf algebra over $R$ and $G$ is a group, then every element of the image of $G$ in $A[G]$ is group-like.
nodes.label: 0-grp-like-grp-alg-of

nodes.statement: This is an easy check.
If $R$ is a commutative semiring, $A$ is a Hopf algebra over $R$ and $G$ is a group, then the group-like elements in $A[G]$ span $A[G]$ as an $A$-module.
nodes.label: 0-grp-like-grp-alg-span

nodes.statement: This follows immediately from \ref{0-grp-like-grp-alg-of}.

nodes.name: Independence of group-like elements
nodes.statement: The group-like elements in a bialgebra $A$ over a domain are linearly independent.
nodes.label: 0-grp-like-lin-indep

nodes.statement:
Let's prove that any finite set $s$ of group-like elements is linearly independent, by induction on $s$. $\emptyset$ is clearly linearly independent. Assume now that the finite set $s$ of group-like elements is linearly independent, that $a 
otin s$ is group-like, and let's show that $s \cup \{a\}$ is linearly independent too. Assume there is some $c : A 	o R$ such that $\sum_{x \in s} c_x x = c_a a$. Since $a$ and all elements of $s$ are group-like, we compute  egin{align*} \sum_{x, y \in s} c_x c_y x \otimes y & = c_a ^ 2 a \otimes a \ & = c_a ^ 2 \Delta(a) \ & = c_a \Delta\left(\sum_{x \in s} c_x xight) \ & = \sum_{x \in s} c_a c_x \Delta(x) \ & = \sum_{x \in s} c_a c_x x \otimes x \end{align*} By Lemma ef{0-tensor-lin-indep}, the $x \otimes y$ are linearly independent and therefore $c_x ^ 2 = c_a c_x$ and $c_x c_y = 0$ if $x 
e y$. If $c_x = 0$ for all $x \in s$, then we are clearly done. Else find $x \in s$ such that $c_x 
e 0$. From the above two equations, we get that $c_x = c_a$ and $c_y = 0$ for all $y \in s, y 
e x$. Therefore \[c_x x = \sum_{y \in s} c_y y = c_a a = c_x a\] and $x = a$. Contradiction.

nodes.name: Group-like elements in a group algebra
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a domain. The group-like elements of $R[M]$ are exactly the image of $M$.
nodes.label: 0-grp-like-grp-alg

nodes.statement: See Lemma 12.4 in \cite{Milne_2017}.

nodes.name: Galois connection between group algebra and group-like elements
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a domain, $G$ a commutative group and $A$ a $R$-bialgebra. Then bialgebra homs $R[G] \to A$ are in bijection with group homs $G \to \mathrm{GrpLike} A$.
nodes.label: 0-grp-alg-grp-like-gc

nodes.statement: If $f : G \to \mathrm{GrpLike} A$ is a group hom, then we get \begin{align*} R[G] \to A g \mapsto f(g) \end{align*} This is clearly an algebra hom, so for it to be a bialgebra hom we only need to check comultiplication is preserved. We only need to check this on $g \in G$, in which case \[(f \otimes f)(\Delta(g)) = (f \otimes f)(g \otimes g) = f(g) \otimes f(g) = \Delta(f(g))\] since $f(g) \in \mathrm{GrpLike} A$. If $f : R[G] \to A$ is a bialgebra hom, then it restricts to a group hom $\mathrm{GrpLike} R[G] \to \mathrm{GrpLike} A$ by Proposition \ref{0-grp-like-map}. Now use that $\mathrm{GrpLike} R[G] \cong G$ from Proposition \ref{0-grp-like-grp-alg}.

nodes.name: Quotients by binomial ideals
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a Hopf algebra, $H$ be a subgroup of $\mathrm{GrpLike} A$ and \[ I = \langle h_1 - h_2 : h_1,h_2 \in H \rangle \] be an ideal. Then $I$ is a Hopf ideal.
nodes.label: 0-grp-like-quot-hopf

nodes.statement: It suffices to check the conditions of a Hopf ideal on generators. For the comultiplication condition: \begin{align*} \Delta(h_1-h_2) &= \Delta(h_1) - \Delta(h_2) \\ &= h_1 \otimes h_1 - h_2 \otimes h_2 \\ &= h_1 \otimes h_1 - h_1 \otimes h_2 + h_1 \otimes h_2 - h_2 \otimes h_2 \\ &= h_1 \otimes (h_1 - h_2) + (h_1 - h_2) \otimes h_2 \in \bar{A \otimes I} + \bar{I \otimes A}. \end{align*} For the counit condition: \[ \varepsilon(h_1 - h_2) = \varepsilon(h_1) - \varepsilon(h_2) = 1 - 1 = 0. \] Finally, for the antipode condition: \[ S(h_1 - h_2) = S(h_1) - S(h_2) = h_1^{-1} - h_2^{-1} \in I. \]

nodes.name: Diagonalizable bialgebras
nodes.statement: A bialgebra is called diagonalizable if it is isomorphic to a group algebra.
nodes.label: 0-is-diag-bialg

nodes.statement: A diagonalizable bialgebra is spanned by its group-like elements.
nodes.label: 0-is-diag-bialg-group-like-span

nodes.statement: This is true for a group algebra by \ref{0-grp-like-grp-alg-span}, and the property of being spanned by its group-like elements is preserves by isomorphisms of bialgebras.

Let $A$ be a bialgebra over a domain $R$, let $G$ be a subgroup of $\mathrm{GrpLike}(A)$ (which is a monoid by \ref{0-grp-like-grp}). If $A$ is generated by $G$, then the unique bialgebra morphism from $R[G]$ to $A$ sending each element of $G$ to itself is bijective.
nodes.label: 0-bialg-bij-of-span-grp-like

nodes.statement: This morphism is injective by the linear independence of group-like elements (\ref{0-grp-like-lin-indep}), and surjective by assumption.

nodes.name: Quotient of a diagonalisable bialgebra is diagonalisable
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a domain, $G$ a commutative group, $A$ a $R$-bialgebra and $f : R[G] \to A$ a surjective bialgebra hom. Then $R[f(G)] \cong A$ as bialgebras.
nodes.label: 0-is-diag-bialg-quot

nodes.statement: Note that $R[G] \xrightarrow f A$ factors as $R[G] \xrightarrow f R[f(G)] \xrightarrow\phi A$, where $f(G)$ is a group by Proposition \ref{0-grp-like-grp}. Since $R[G] \xrightarrow f A$ is surjective, so is $R[f(G)] \xrightarrow\phi A$. Therefore Proposition \ref{0-bialg-bij-of-span-grp-like} applies to $f(G)$ inside $A$, and we get $R[f(G)] \cong A$.
A bialgebra over a domain is diagonalizable if and only if it is spanned by its group-like elements.
nodes.label: 0-is-diag-bialg-iff-span-group-like

nodes.statement: We know that a diagonalizable bialgebra is spanned by its group-like elements by \ref{0-is-diag-bialg-group-like-span}, and that a bialgebra over a domain that is spanned by its group-like elements is diagonalizable by \ref{0-is-diag-bialg-quot} (and by the fact that a bijective morphism of bialgebras is an isomorphism).

nodes.name: The antipode is a antihomomorphism
nodes.statement: If $A$ is a $R$-Hopf algebra, then the antipode map $s : A \to A$ is anti-commutative, ie $s(a * b) = s(b) * s(a)$. If further $A$ is commutative, then $s(a * b) = s(a) * s(b)$.
nodes.label: 0-antipode-mul

nodes.statement: Any standard reference will have a proof.

nodes.name: Bialgebras are comonoid objects in the category of algebras
nodes.statement: The category of $R$-bialgebras is equivalent to comonoid objects in the category of $R$-algebras.
nodes.label: 0-bialg-equiv-comon-alg

nodes.statement: Turn the arrows around.

nodes.name: Hopf algebras are cogroup objects in the category of algebras
nodes.statement: The category of $R$-Hopf algebras is equivalent to cogroup objects in the category of $R$-algebras.
nodes.label: 0-hopf-alg-equiv-cogrp-alg

nodes.statement: Turn the arrows around. Most of the diagrams have been turned around in Proposition \ref{0-bialg-equiv-comon-alg} already.

nodes.name: The group algebra functor
nodes.statement: For a commutative ring $R$, we have a functor $G \rightsquigarrow R[G] : \mathrm{Grp} \to \mathrm{Hopf}_R$.
nodes.label: 0-grp-alg

nodes.name: The group algebra functor is fully faithful
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a domain. The functor $G \rightsquigarrow R[G]$ from the category of groups to the category of Hopf algebras over $R$ is fully faithful.
nodes.label: 0-full-faithful-grp-alg

nodes.statement: The functor is clearly faithful. Now for the full part, if $f : R[G] \to R[H]$ is a Hopf algebra hom, then we get a series of maps \[ G \simeq \text{ group-like elements of } R[G] \to \text{ group-like elements of } R[H] \simeq H \] and each map separately is clearly multiplicative.

nodes.name: Convex cone generated by a set
nodes.statement: For a set $S \subseteq N$, the {\bf cone generated by $S$}, aka {\bf cone hull of $S$}, is $$\mathrm{Cone}(S) := \left\{\sum_{u \in S} \lambda_u u | \lambda_u \ge 0\right\}$$
nodes.label: 1-2-1-cone-hull

nodes.name: Convex polyhedral cone
nodes.statement: A {\bf polyhedral cone} is a set that can be written as $\mathrm{Cone}(S)$ for some finite set $S$.
nodes.label: 1-2-1-polyhedral-cone

nodes.name: Convex hull
nodes.statement: For a set $S \subseteq N$, the {\bf convex hull of $S$} is $$\mathrm{Conv}(S) := \left\{\sum_{u \in S} \lambda_u | \lambda_u \ge 0, \sum_u \lambda_u = 1\right\}$$
nodes.label: 1-2-2-convex-hull

nodes.name: Polytope
nodes.statement: A {\bf polytope} is a set that can be written as $\mathrm{Conv}(S)$ for some finite set $S$.
nodes.label: 1-2-2-polytope

nodes.name: Dual cone
nodes.statement: Given a polyhedral cone $\sigma \subseteq N$, its {\bf dual cone} is defined by $$\sigma^\vee = \{m \in M | \forall u \in \sigma, \langle m, u\rangle \ge 0\}$$.
nodes.label: 1-2-3-dual-cone

nodes.name: Dual of a polyhedral cone
nodes.statement: If $\sigma$ is polyhedral, then its dual $\sigma^\vee$ is polyhedral too.
nodes.label: 1-2-4-dual-polyhedral-cone

nodes.statement: Classic, use Fourier-Motzkin eliminiation.

nodes.name: Dual cone of a sumset
nodes.statement: If $\sigma_1, \sigma_2$ are two cones, then $$(\sigma_1 + \sigma_2)^\vee = \sigma_1^\vee \cap \sigma_2^\vee.$$
nodes.label: 1-2-dual-cone-add

nodes.statement: Classic. See \cite{Oda_1988} maybe.

nodes.name: Double dual of a polyhedral cone
nodes.statement: If $\sigma$ is polyhedral, then $\sigma^{\vee\vee} = \sigma$.
nodes.label: 1-2-4-double-dual-polyhedral-cone

nodes.statement: Classic. See \cite{Oda_1988} maybe.

nodes.name: Face of a cone
nodes.statement: If $\sigma$ is a cone, then a subset of $\sigma$ is a {\bf face} iff it is the intersection of $\sigma$ with some halfspace. We write this $\tau \preceq \sigma$. If furthermore $\tau \ne \sigma$, we call $\tau$ a proper face and write $\tau \prec \sigma$.
nodes.label: 1-2-5-face

nodes.name: Edge of a cone
nodes.statement: A dimension 1 face of a cone is called an \emph{edge}.
nodes.label: 1-2-5-edge

nodes.name: Facet of a cone
nodes.statement: A codimension 1 face of a cone is called a \emph{facet}.
nodes.label: 1-2-5-facet

nodes.name: Face of a polyhedral cone
nodes.statement: If $\sigma$ is a polyhedral cone, then every face of $\sigma$ is a polyhedral cone.
nodes.label: 1-2-6-face-polyhedral-cone

nodes.name: Intersection of faces
nodes.statement: If $\sigma$ is a polyhedral cone, then the intersection of two faces of $\sigma$ is a face of $\sigma$.
nodes.label: 1-2-6-inter-faces

nodes.statement: Classic. See \cite{Oda_1988} maybe.

nodes.name: Face of a face
nodes.statement: A face of a face of a polyhedral cone $\sigma$ is again a face of $\sigma$.
nodes.label: 1-2-6-face-face

nodes.statement: Classic. See \cite{Oda_1988} maybe.
Let $\tau$ be a face of a polyhedral cone $\sigma$. If $v, w \in \sigma$ and $v + w \in \tau$, then $v, w \in \tau$.
nodes.label: 1-2-7-face-mem-of-add

nodes.statement: Classic. See \cite{Oda_1988} maybe.

nodes.name: Dual cone of the intersection of halfspaces
nodes.statement: If $\sigma = H_{m_1}^+ \cap \dots \cap H_{m_s}^+$, then $$\sigma^\vee = \mathrm{Cone}(m_1, \dots, m_s).$$
nodes.label: 1-2-8-dual-cone-inter-halfspaces

nodes.statement: Classic. See \cite{Oda_1988} maybe.

nodes.name: Facets of a full dimensional cone
nodes.statement: If $\sigma$ is a full dimensional cone, then facets of $\sigma$ are of the form $H_m \cap \sigma$.
nodes.label: 1-2-8-facet-full-dim-cone

nodes.statement: Classic. See \cite{Oda_1988} maybe.

nodes.name: Intersection of facets containing a face
nodes.statement: Every proper face $\tau \prec \sigma$ of a polyhedral cone $\sigma$ is the intersection of the facets of $\sigma$ containing $\tau$.
nodes.label: 1-2-8-inter-facet

nodes.statement: Classic. See \cite{Oda_1988} maybe.

nodes.name: Dual face
nodes.statement: Given a cone $\sigma$ and a face $\tau \preceq \sigma$, the {\bf dual face} to $\tau$ is $$\tau^* := \sigma^\vee \cap \tau^\perp$$
nodes.label: 1-2-10-dual-face

nodes.name: The dual face is a face of the dual
nodes.statement: If $\tau \preceq \sigma$, then $\tau^* \preceq \sigma^\vee$.
nodes.label: 1-2-10-dual-face-face-dual

nodes.statement: Classic. See \cite{Oda_1988} maybe.

nodes.name: The double dual of a face
nodes.statement: If $\tau \preceq \sigma$, then $\tau^{**} = \tau$.
nodes.label: 1-2-10-double-dual-face-dual-face

nodes.statement: Classic. See \cite{Oda_1988} maybe.

nodes.name: The dual of a face is antitone
nodes.statement: If $\tau' \preceq \tau \preceq \sigma$, then $\tau' \preceq \tau$.
nodes.label: 1-2-10-dual-face-antitone

nodes.statement: Classic. See \cite{Oda_1988} maybe.

nodes.name: The dimension of the dual of a face
nodes.statement: If $\tau \preceq \sigma$, then $$\dim \tau + \dim \tau^* = \dim N.$$
nodes.label: 1-2-10-dim-dual-face

nodes.statement: Classic. See \cite{Oda_1988} maybe.

nodes.name: Relative interior
nodes.statement: The {\bf relative interior}, aka {\bf intrinsic interior}, of a cone $\sigma$ is the interior of $\sigma$ as a subset of its span.
nodes.label: 1-2-rel-interior

nodes.name: The relative interior in terms of the inner product
nodes.statement: For a cone $\sigma$, $$u \in \mathrm{Relint}(\sigma) \iff \forall m \in \sigma^\vee \setminus \sigma^\perp, \langle m, u\rangle > 0$$
nodes.label: 1-2-rel-interior-inner

nodes.statement: Classic. See \cite{Oda_1988} maybe.

nodes.name: Relative interior of a dual face
nodes.statement: If $\tau \preceq \sigma$ and $m \in \sigma^\vee$, then $$m \in \mathrm{Relint}(\tau^*) \iff \tau = H_m \cap \sigma$$
nodes.label: 1-2-rel-interior-dual-face

nodes.statement: Classic. See \cite{Oda_1988} maybe.

nodes.name: Minimal face of a cone
nodes.statement: If $\sigma$ is a cone, then $W := \sigma \cap (-\sigma)$ is a subspace. Furthermore, $W = H_m \cap \sigma$ whenever $m \in \mathrm{Relint}(\sigma^\vee)$.
nodes.label: 1-2-min-face

nodes.statement: Classic. See \cite{Oda_1988} maybe.

nodes.name: Salient cones
nodes.statement: A cone $\sigma$ is {\bf salient}, aka {\bf pointed} or {\bf strongly convex}, if $\sigma \cap (-\sigma) = \{0\}$.
nodes.label: 1-2-12-salient-cone

nodes.name: Alternative definitions of salient cones
nodes.statement: The following are equivalent \begin{enumerate} \item $\sigma$ is salient \item $\{0\} \preceq \sigma$ \item $\sigma$ contains no positive dimensional subspace \item $\dim \sigma^\vee = \dim N$ \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: 1-2-12-salient-cone-tfae

nodes.statement: Classic. See \cite{Oda_1988} maybe.

nodes.name: Separation lemma
nodes.statement: Let $\sigma_1, \sigma_2$ be polyhedral cones meeting along a common face $\tau$. Then $$\tau = H_m \cap \sigma_1 = H_m \cap \sigma_2$$ for any $m \in \mathrm{Relint}(\sigma_1^\vee \cap (-\sigma_2)^\vee)$.
nodes.label: 1-2-13-separation-lemma

nodes.statement: See \cite{Cox_2011}.

nodes.name: Rational cone
nodes.statement: A cone $\sigma \subseteq N_{\mathbb R}$ is {\bf rational} if $\sigma = \mathrm{Cone}(S)$ for some finite set $S \subseteq N$.
nodes.label: 1-2-14-rat-cone

nodes.name: Faces of a rational cone
nodes.statement: If $\tau \preceq \sigma$ is a face of a rational cone, then $\tau$ itself is rational.
nodes.label: 1-2-14-face-rat-cone

nodes.statement: Classic. See \cite{Oda_1988} maybe.

nodes.name: The dual of a rational cone
nodes.statement: $\sigma^\vee$ is a rational cone iff $\sigma$ is.
nodes.label: 1-2-14-dual-rat-cone

nodes.statement: Classic. See \cite{Oda_1988} maybe.

nodes.name: Ray generator
nodes.statement: If $\rho$ is an edge of a rational cone $\sigma$, then the monoid $\rho \cap N$ is generated by a unique element $u_\rho \in \rho \cap N$, which we call the {\bf ray generator} of $\rho$.
nodes.label: 1-2-ray-gen

nodes.name: Minimal generators
nodes.statement: The {\bf minimal generators} of a rational cone $\sigma$ are the ray generators of its edges.
nodes.label: 1-2-min-gen

nodes.name: A rational cone is generated by its minimal generators
nodes.statement: A salient convex rational polyhedral cone is generated by its minimal generators.
nodes.label: 1-2-15-cone-hull-min-gen

nodes.statement: Classic. See \cite{Oda_1988} maybe.

nodes.name: Regular cone
nodes.statement: A salient rational polyhedral cone $\sigma$ is {\bf regular}, aka {\bf smooth}, if its minimal generators form part of a ${\mathbb Z}$-basis of $N$.
nodes.label: 1-2-16-reg-cone

nodes.name: Simplicial cone
nodes.statement: A salient rational polyhedral cone $\sigma$ is {\bf simplicial} if its minimal generators are ${\mathbb R}$-linearly independent.
nodes.label: 1-2-16-simplicial-cone

nodes.name: Dual lattice of a cone
nodes.statement: If $\sigma \subseteq N_{\mathbb R}$ is a polyhedral cone, then the lattice points \[ S_\sigma := \sigma^\vee \cap M \] form a monoid.
nodes.label: 1-2-17-dual-lat-cone

nodes.name: Gordan's lemma
nodes.statement: $S_\sigma$ is finitely generated as a monoid.
nodes.label: 1-2-17-gordan-lemma

nodes.statement: See \cite{Cox_2011}.

nodes.name: Affine toric variety of a rational polyhedral cone
nodes.statement: $U_\sigma := \mathrm{Spec} {\mathbb C}[S_\sigma]$ is an affine toric variety.
nodes.label: 1-2-18-aff-tor-var-rat-polyhedral-cone

nodes.name: Dimension of the affine toric variety of a rational polyhedral cone
nodes.statement: \[ \dim U_\sigma = \dim N \iff \text{ the torus of $U_\sigma$ is } T_N = N \otimes_[{\mathbb Z}] {\mathbb C}^* \iff \sigma \text{ is salient}. \]
nodes.label: 1-2-18-dim-aff-tor-var-rat-polyhedral-cone

nodes.statement: See \cite{Cox_2011}.

nodes.name: The irreducible elements of the dual lattice of a cone
nodes.statement: If $\sigma \subseteq N_{\mathbb R}$ is salient of maximal dimension, then the irreducible elements of $S_\sigma$ are precisely the minimal generators of $\sigma^\vee$.
nodes.label: 1-2-22-irred-dual-lat

nodes.statement: See \cite{Cox_2011}.

nodes.name: The diagonalisable group scheme functor
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a commutative group and $S$ a base scheme. The diagonalisable group scheme $D_S(G)$ is defined as the base-change of $\mathrm{Spec} {\mathbb Z}[G]$ to $S$. For a commutative ring $R$, we write $D_R(G) := D_{\mathrm{Spec} R}(G)$.
nodes.label: 0-diag

nodes.name: Diagonalisable group schemes
nodes.statement: An algebraic group $G$ over $\mathrm{Spec} R$ is {\bf diagonalisable} if it is isomorphic to $D_R(G)$ for some commutative group $G$.
nodes.label: 0-is-diag

nodes.name: The diagonalisable group scheme torus over $\Spec R$
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $M$ an abelian monoid. Then $D_R(M)$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{Spec} R[M]$.
nodes.label: 0-diag-spec

nodes.statement: Ask any toddler on the street.
An algebraic group $G$ over a field $k$ is diagonalizable if and only if $\Gamma(G)$ is spanned by its group-like elements.
nodes.label: 0-diag-iff-grp-like-span

nodes.statement: See Theorem 12.8 in \cite{Milne_2017}.
Let $R$ be a domain. The functor $D_R(G) := G \rightsquigarrow \mathrm{Spec} R[G]$ from the category of groups to the category of group schemes over $\mathrm{Spec} R$ is fully faithful.
nodes.label: 0-full-faithful-diag

nodes.statement: Compose Propositions \ref{0-full-faithful-spec-hopf} and \ref{0-full-faithful-grp-alg}. Also see Theorem 12.9(a) in \cite{Milne_2017}. See SGA III Exposé VIII for a proof that works for $R$ an arbitrary commutative ring.

nodes.name: Morphisms between diagonalisable group schemes are affine
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a scheme. Let $M, N$ be commutative monoids and $f : M \to N$ a monoid hom. Then the map $D_S(f) : D_S(N) \to D_S(M)$ is affine.
nodes.label: 0-diag-aff-hom

nodes.statement: $\mathrm{Spec} f : \mathrm{Spec} {\mathbb Z}[N] \to \mathrm{Spec} {\mathbb Z}[M]$ is affine, since it's a morphism of affine schemes. Therefore $D_S(f)$ is affine, as affine morphisms are preserved under base change.

nodes.name: Closed embeddings between diagonalisable group schemes
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a scheme. Let $M, N$ be commutative monoids and $f : M \to N$ a surjective monoid hom. Then the map $D_S(f) : D_S(N) \to D_S(M)$ is a closed embedding.
nodes.label: 0-diag-closed-emb

nodes.statement: Since $f$ is surjective, the corresponding map $\hat f : {\mathbb Z}[M] \to {\mathbb Z}[N]$ is surjective too. Hence $\mathrm{Spec} \hat f : \mathrm{Spec} {\mathbb Z}[N] \to \mathrm{Spec} {\mathbb Z}[M]$ is a closed embedding. Therefore $D_S(f)$ is a closed embedding, as closed embeddings are preserved under base change.

nodes.name: Faithfully flat morphisms between diagonalisable group schemes
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a scheme. Let $G, H$ be abelian groups and $f : G \to H$ an injective group hom. Then the map $D_S(f) : D_S(H) \to D_S(G)$ is faithfully flat.
nodes.label: 0-diag-faithful-flat

nodes.statement: Since $f$ is injective, ${\mathbb Z}[H]$ is a free module over ${\mathbb Z}[G]$ by Proposition \ref{0-grp-alg-free}, hence the map ${\mathbb Z}[G] \to {\mathbb Z}[H]$ is faithfully flat and so is $\mathrm{Spec} {\mathbb Z}[H] \to \mathrm{Spec} {\mathbb Z}[G]$. Therefore $D_S(f)$ is faithfully flat, as faithfully flat morphisms are preserved under base change.

nodes.name: A subgroup of a diagonalisable group scheme is a diagonalisable group scheme
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a domain. Let $G$ be an abelian group. If $H$ is a closed subgroup of $D_R(G)$, then $H$ is a diagonalisable group scheme.
nodes.label: 0-subgroup-diag

nodes.statement: $H$ is a closed subscheme of an affine scheme, hence it is affine. By Proposition \ref{0-ess-image-spec-hopf}, write $H = \mathrm{Spec} A$ where $A$ is a $R$-Hopf algebra. The closed subgroup embedding $H \hookrightarrow D_R(G)$ becomes a surjective bialgebra hom $R[G] \to A$ by Propositions \ref{0-diag-spec} and \ref{0-full-faithful-spec-hopf}. By Proposition \ref{0-is-diag-bialg-quot}, $A$ is a diagonalisable bialgebra and therefore $H$ is a diagonalisable group scheme.

nodes.name: Diagonalisable group scheme of a torsion group is disconnected
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be an abelian group with an element of torsion $n$. Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $n$ invertible. Then $D_R(G)$ is disconnected.
nodes.label: 0-diag-tors

nodes.statement: Say $x \in G$ is such that $x^n = 1$. Then \[e : R[G] := \frac 1n \sum_{i = 0}^n x^i\] is such that $e ^ 2 = e$. We are done by Proposition \ref{0-diag-spec}.

nodes.name: The split torus
nodes.statement: The split torus ${\mathbb G}_m^n$ over a scheme $S$ is the pullback of $\mathrm{Spec} {\mathbb Z}[x_1^{\pm 1}, \dotsc, x_n^{\pm 1}]$ along the unique map $S \to \mathrm{Spec} {\mathbb Z}$.
nodes.label: 0-torus

nodes.name: Diag is a group isomorphism on hom sets
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a domain. The functor $G \rightsquigarrow \mathrm{Spec} R[G]$ from the category of groups to the category of group schemes over $\mathrm{Spec} R$ is a group isomorphism on hom sets.
nodes.label: 0-diag-hom

nodes.statement: Toddlers and streets by Lemmas \ref{0-full-faithful-diag} and \ref{0-full-faithful-grp-hom}.

nodes.name: Characters of a group scheme
nodes.statement: For a group scheme $G$ over $S$, the {\bf character lattice} of $G$ is \[ X(G) := \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathsf{GrpSch}_S}(G, {\mathbb G}_m). \] An element of $X(G)$ is called a {\bf character}.
nodes.label: 0-char

nodes.name: Cocharacters of a group scheme
nodes.statement: For a group scheme $G$ over $S$, the {\bf cocharacter lattice} of $G$ is \[ X^*(G) := \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathsf{GrpSch}_S}({\mathbb G}_m, G). \] An element of $X^*(G)$ is called a {\bf cocharacter} or {\bf one-parameter subgroup}.
nodes.label: 0-cochar

nodes.name: Character lattice of a diagonalisable group scheme
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a domain and $G$ be a commutative group. Then $X(\mathrm{Spec} R[G]) = G$.
nodes.label: 0-char-diag

nodes.statement: By Propositions \ref{0-diag-spec} and \ref{0-full-faithful-diag} in turn, we have \[ X(G) = \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathsf{GrpSch}}(G, {\mathbb G}_m) = \mathrm{Hom}(k[{\mathbb Z}], k[G]) = \mathrm{Hom}({\mathbb Z}, G) = G. \]

nodes.name: Cocharacter lattice of a diagonalisable group scheme
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a domain and $G$ be a commutative group. Then $X^*(\mathrm{Spec} R[G]) = \mathrm{Hom}(G, {\mathbb Z})$.
nodes.label: 0-cochar-diag

nodes.statement: By Propositions \ref{0-diag-spec} and \ref{0-full-faithful-diag} in turn, we have \[ X^*(G) = \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathsf{GrpSch}}({\mathbb G}_m, G) = \mathrm{Hom}(k[G], k[{\mathbb Z}]) = \mathrm{Hom}(G, {\mathbb Z}). \]

nodes.name: Character lattice of the torus
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a torus of dimension $n$ over a domain $R$. Then $X(G) = {\mathbb Z}^n$.
nodes.label: 0-char-torus

nodes.statement: Immediate from Propositions \ref{0-diag-spec} and \ref{0-char-diag}.

nodes.name: Cocharacter lattice of the torus
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a torus of dimension $n$ over a domain $R$. Then $X^*(G) = \mathrm{Hom}({\mathbb Z}^n, {\mathbb Z})$.
nodes.label: 0-cochar-torus

nodes.statement: Immediate from Propositions \ref{0-diag-spec} and \ref{0-cochar-diag}.

nodes.name: The character-cocharacter pairing
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a domain and $G$ a group scheme over $\mathrm{Spec} R$. Then there is a ${\mathbb Z}$-valued perfect pairing between $X(G)$ and $X^*(G)$.
nodes.label: 0-char-cochar-pairing

nodes.name: The character-cocharacter pairing is perfect
nodes.statement: The character-cocharacter pairing on a torus is perfect.
nodes.label: 0-char-cochar-pairing-perfect

nodes.statement: Transfer everything across the isos $X({\mathbb G}_m^n) = {\mathbb Z}^n, X*({\mathbb G}_m^n) = \mathrm{Hom}({\mathbb Z}^n, {\mathbb Z})$.

nodes.name: The image of a torus is a torus
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a domain. Let $T$ be a split torus over $R$. Let $G$ be a diagonalisable group scheme over $R$ and let $\phi: T \to G$ be a homomorphism. Then the (scheme theoretic) image of $\phi$ is a split torus over $R$ and the maps \[ T \xrightarrow{\hat{\phi}} \operatorname{im}\phi \xrightarrow{\iota} G \] are group homomorphisms, and $\hat{\phi}$ is fpqc. Furthermore, if $T = D_R(H), G = D_R(I), \phi = D_R(f)$ for $H$ a finitely generated free abelian group, $I$ an abelian group, $f : I \to H$ a group hom, then $\operatorname{im} \phi \cong D_R(\operatorname{im}(f))$.
nodes.label: 1-1-1-group-hom-torus

nodes.statement: By fullness of $D_R$ (Proposition \ref{0-full-faithful-diag}), it's enough to handle the case where $T = D_R(H), G = D_R(I), \phi = D_R(f)$ for $H$ a finitely generated free abelian group, $I$ an abelian group, $f : I \to H$ a group hom. Then $\operatorname{im}(f)$ is a subgroup of the finitely-generated free abelian group $H$, hence itself a finitely-generated free abelian group (since free is equivalent to torsion-free for finitely-generated abelian groups, and a subgroup of a torsion-free group is torsion-free).

nodes.name: A subgroup of a torus is a torus
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring of characteristic zero. Let $T$ be a split torus. If $H \subseteq T$ is a connected closed subgroup, then $H$ is a split torus.
nodes.label: 1-1-1-subgroup-torus

nodes.statement: By assumption, write $T \cong D_k[G]$ for $G$ a free abelian group. By Proposition \ref{0-subgroup-diag}, $H$ is a diagonalisable group scheme, say $H \cong D_k(I)$ for $I$ an abelian group. Since $H$ is a closed subscheme, the map $G \to I$ is surjective, so $I$ is a finitely-generated abelian group. Since $H$ is connected, Proposition \ref{0-diag-tors} says $I$ is torsion-free, hence free. Thus $H$ is a split torus.

nodes.name: Toric varieties
nodes.statement: Let $k$ be a field. Let $T$ be a torus over $k$. A \emph{toric variety} structure on a scheme $X$ over $k$ consists the following data: \begin{itemize} \item a torus $T$ over $k$, \item a group action $T \times X \to X$ over $k$. \item a dominant open immersion $i : T \hookrightarrow X$ over $k$ that is $T$-equivariant. \end{itemize}
nodes.label: 5-1-tor-var

nodes.name: Torus morphisms, torus isomorphisms
nodes.statement: Let $k$ be a field. Let $T_1, T_2$ be tori over $k$. Let $X_1, X_2$ be toric varieties with torus $T_1, T_2$ respectively. A \emph{toric morphism} from $X_1$ to $X_2$ is the data of a $k$-morphism $X_1 \to X_2$ and a $k$-group homomorphism $T_1 \to T_2$ that commute with the embeddings $T_1 \to X_1, T_2 \to X_2$ and the actions. A \emph{toric isomorphism} from $X_1$ to $X_2$ is the data of two isomorphisms $X_1 \cong X_2$ and $T_1 \cong T_2$ that commute with the embeddings $T_1 \to X_1, T_2 \to X_2$.
nodes.label: 5-1-tor-hom

nodes.name: The diagonalisable group scheme of an affine monoid algebra is an affine toric variety
nodes.statement: Let $k$ be a field. Let $G$ be a finitely generated free abelian group. Let $M$ be an affine monoid with Grothendieck group $G$. Then $D_k(M)$ is an affine toric variety over $k$ with torus $D_k(G)$.
nodes.section: 5.2 Affine toric varieties and affine monoids
nodes.label: 1-1-aff-tor-var-diag-aff-mon

nodes.statement: The map $D_k(G) \hookrightarrow D_k(M)$ is given by the embedding $M \hookrightarrow G$. We identify $D_k(G) \cong \mathrm{Spec} k[G], D_k(M) \cong \mathrm{Spec} k[M]$ using Proposition \ref{0-diag-spec}. By Proposition \ref{0-loc-mon-alg}, $k[G]$ is a localization of $k[M]$. Therefore the map $\mathrm{Spec} k[G] \hookrightarrow \mathrm{Spec} k[M]$ is an open immersion. This open immersion is dominant since $\mathrm{Spec} k[M]$ is irreducible as $k[M]$ is a domain (Proposition \ref{0-aff-mon-alg-domain}). The group action $D_k(G) \times D_k(M) \to D_k(M)$ comes from pulling back along $D_k(G) \hookrightarrow D_k(M)$ the left action $D_k(M) \times D_k(M) \to D_k(M)$ using Proposition \ref{0-comap-mod}.
nodes.section: 5.2 Affine toric varieties and affine monoids

nodes.name: The character eigenspace
nodes.statement: For a finite dimensional representation of a torus $T$ on $W$, the {\bf character eigenspace} of a character $\chi \in X(T)$ is \[ W_m = \{w\in W : t\cdot w = \chi(t)\text{ for all } t\in T \}. \]

nodes.name: Lattice ideal
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $G$ be a free abelian group and $M$ an affine monoid whose Grothendieck group is $G$. Let $L \le G$ be a sublattice. The \emph{lattice ideal} of $L$ is the $R$-ideal of $R[M]$ defined by \[ I_L := \langle X^\alpha - X^\beta | \alpha, \beta \in M, \alpha - \beta \in L\rangle. \]

nodes.name: An ideal is toric iff it is prime and generated by binomials
nodes.statement: An ideal is toric if and only if it's prime and generated by binomials $X^\alpha - X^\beta$.
nodes.section: 5.3 Affine toric varieties and toric ideals
nodes.label: 1-1-11-toric-ideal-gen-binomial

nodes.statement: A toric ideal is prime and generated by binomials by definition. Assume $I$ is prime and generated by $X^\alpha - X^\beta$ ranging over $(\alpha, \beta) \in S$ for some set $S \subseteq M \times M$. Note first that $I$ doesn't contain any monomial. Indeed, $I$ is contained in the kernel of the map $R[M] \to R$ given by $X^m \mapsto 1$. Since $I$ is prime, this means that \[ X^{\alpha + \gamma} - X^{\beta + \gamma} \in I \iff X^\alpha - X^\beta \in I. \] In particular, if $\alpha_1 - \beta_1 = \alpha_2 - \beta_2$, then Since $I$ is prime, this means that \[ X^{\alpha_1} - X^{\beta_1} \in I \iff X^{\alpha_1 + \beta_2} - X^{\beta_1 + \beta_2} \in I \iff X^{\alpha_2 + \beta_1} - X^{\beta_1 + \beta_2} \in I \iff X^{\alpha_2} - X^{\beta_2} \in I. \] Now, we claim that $I = I_L$ where $L \le G$ is given by \[ \mathrm{span}\{\delta - \varepsilon | (\delta, \varepsilon) \in S\}. \] Clearly, $I \subseteq I_L$. For the other direction, assume $\delta, \varepsilon \in M, \delta - \varepsilon \in L$. Let's prove $X^\delta - X^\varepsilon \in I$ by induction on $\delta - \varepsilon \in L$: \begin{itemize} \item If $\delta - \varepsilon = 0$, then $X^\delta - X^\varepsilon = 0 \in I$. \item If $\delta_1 - \varepsilon_1 = \varepsilon_2 - \delta_2$ and $X^{\delta_2} - X^{\varepsilon_2} \in I$, then \[ X^{\delta_1} - X^{\varepsilon_1} \in I \iff X^{\varepsilon_2} - X^{\delta_2} \iff X^{\delta_1} - X^{\varepsilon_1} \] by the remark, and this holds by assumption. \item If $\delta - \varepsilon = \alpha - \beta$ where $(\alpha, \beta) \in S$, then \[ X^\delta - X^\varepsilon \in I \iff X^\alpha - X^\beta \in I \] by the remark, and this holds by assumption. \item Assume $\delta_1, \delta_2, \varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2$ are such that $X^{\delta_1} - X^{\varepsilon_1}, X^{\delta_2} - X^{\varepsilon_2} \in I$. Then \[ X^{\delta_1 + \delta_2} - X^{\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2} = (X^{\delta_1} - X^{\varepsilon_1})X^{\delta_2} + X^{\varepsilon_1}(X^{\delta_2} - X^{\varepsilon_2}) \in I. \] \end{itemize}

nodes.statement: {\textbf Torus: } Define the torus $T'$ to be the one we get from \ref{1-1-1-group-hom-torus} with quotient map $\pi:T \to T'$. {\textbf Open embedding: } Since both $Y_{{\mathcal A}},T'$ are closures of $\Phi,\Phi'$ and ${\mathbb G}_m^n\to\mathbb{A}^n$ is an open embedding we get an open embedding $\iota:T' \to Y_{{\mathcal A}}$ such that the map $\phi:T \to Y_{{\mathcal A}}$ factors as $\phi = \iota \circ \pi$. {\textbf Dominant: } Since $\phi$ is dominant, so is $\iota$. {\textbf Action: } Since ${\mathbb G}_m^n$ acts on $\mathbb{A}^n$, we get a morphism $a':T' \times_S Y_{\mathcal A} \to \mathbb{A}^n$. As $T'\times_S Y_{\mathcal A}$ is reduced (TODO add lemma), to show that this factors through $Y_{\mathcal A}$ it suffices to check that the image lies in $Y_{\mathcal A}$. First, $T'\times_S T' \to T'\times Y_{\mathcal A}$ is dominant, since $T'$ is flat and flat base change preserves dominance (TODO add lemma). Since the image of $T'\times_S T'$ is $T'$ we're done for topological reasons. {\textbf Equivariant: } The inclusion of the torus is equivariant, since ${\mathbb G}_m^n \to \mathbb{A}^n$ is.
The character lattice of the torus of $Y_{\mathcal A}$ is ${\mathbb Z} {\mathcal A}$.
nodes.label: 1-1-8-char-ya

nodes.statement: $\Phi_{\mathcal A}: T_N \to {\mathbb G}_m^s$ factors through the torus of $Y_{\mathcal A}$. The conclusion follows from looking at the corresponding maps of character lattices.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. Let $G$ be an abelian group. Let $s$ be an arbitrary indexing type, and ${\mathcal A} : s \to G$ an indexed family. Let $L$ be the kernel of $f'_{\mathcal A} : {\mathbb Z}^{\oplus s} \to G$. Then the ideal of the affine toric variety $Y_{\mathcal A}$ is \[ I(Y_{\mathcal A}) = I_L. \]
nodes.label: 1-1-9-ideal-ya

nodes.statement: By the definition of $Y_{\mathcal A}$ as the scheme-theoretic closure of $\Phi_{\mathcal A}$, we have $I(Y_{\mathcal A}) = \ker R[f_{\mathcal A}] = \ker R[f'_{\mathcal A}]$ where, recall, $f_{\mathcal A} : {\mathbb N}^s \to G, f'_{\mathcal A} : {\mathbb Z}^s \to G$ are both given by $e_i \mapsto {\mathcal A}_i$, and $R[f_{\mathcal A}] : R[{\mathbb N}^s] \to R[G]$ is the pushforward. By Proposition \ref{0-ker-mon-alg} with $G := {\mathbb Z}, S := {1}$, \[ \ker R[f_{\mathcal A}] = \mathrm{span}\{X^\alpha - X^\beta | \alpha, \beta \in {\mathbb N}^s, f(\alpha) = f(\beta)\} = \mathrm{span}\{X^\alpha - X^\beta | \alpha, \beta \in {\mathbb N}^s, \alpha - \beta \in L\}. \]
If $S$ is an affine monoid and $\mathcal A$ is a finite set generating $S$ as a monoid, then $\mathrm{Spec} \Bbbk[S] = Y_{\mathcal A}$.
nodes.label: 1-1-14-spec-aff-mon-alg

nodes.statement: We get a $\Bbbk$-algebra homomorphism $\pi : \Bbbk[x_1, \dotsc, x_s] \to \Bbbk[{\mathbb Z} S]$ given by $\mathcal A$; this induces a morphism $\Phi_{\mathcal A} : T \to \Bbbk^s$. The kernel of $\pi$ is the toric ideal of $Y_{\mathcal A}$ and $\pi$ is clearly surjective, so $Y_{\mathcal A} = \mathbb V(\ker(\pi)) = \mathrm{Spec} \Bbbk[x_1, \dotsc, x_s] / \ker(\pi) = \mathrm{Spec} {\mathbb C}[S]$.
The ideal of $Y_{\mathcal A}$ is a toric ideal.
nodes.label: 1-1-10-tor-ideal-ya

nodes.statement: Immediate consequence of Proposition \ref{1-1-9-ideal-ya}.
